headings.title: Introduction to Anatomical Terminology and Body Regions
headings.content: Anatomical terminology provides a universal language for healthcare professionals to describe body structures accurately, preventing confusion during clinical handovers and documentation. The human body is broadly divided into two major divisions: the **axial region** and the **appendicular region**. Standard anatomical position—standing upright, feet flat on the floor, arms at the sides, and palms facing forward—serves as the baseline reference point for all regional descriptions, regardless of the patient's actual posture in bed.

headings.title: Axial Region: Head, Neck, and Trunk
headings.content:
The **axial region** forms the main vertical axis of the human body, supporting the head, neck, and trunk. 

- **Head (cephalic)**: Includes the cranium housing the brain and the facial structures.
- **Neck (cervical)**: Connects the head to the trunk and contains major blood vessels and the trachea.
- **Trunk (torso)**: Divided into the thoracic region (chest), abdominal region, and pelvic region.

headings.title: Appendicular Region: Upper and Lower Limbs
headings.content:
The **appendicular region** consists of the upper and lower limbs, which attach to the axial skeleton via the pectoral and pelvic girdles. 

Upper limbs include the **brachium** (arm), antebrachium (forearm), carpus (wrist), manus (hand), and digits (fingers). Lower limbs include the thigh, crus (leg), tarsus (ankle), pes (foot), and digits (toes). Nurses frequently assess these regions for peripheral pulses, edema, capillary refill, and range of motion during routine physical examinations.

headings.title: Abdominopelvic Regions and Quadrants
headings.content:
To document pain or locate internal organs accurately, healthcare providers divide the large abdominopelvic cavity into either **four quadrants** or **nine regions**. 

The four-quadrant method uses a median and transverse plane crossing at the umbilicus: 
- Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ)
- Left Upper Quadrant (LUQ)
- Right Lower Quadrant (RLQ)
- Left Lower Quadrant (LLQ)

The nine-region method uses two vertical and two horizontal lines, creating areas such as the epigastric, umbilical, and hypogastric regions. Nurses often document acute appendicitis pain as localized tenderness in the right lower quadrant.

headings.title: Anterior and Posterior Surface Landmarks
headings.content: Surface landmarks serve as vital physical guides for palpation, auscultation, and injection placement. **Anterior landmarks** include the sternal angle, umbilicus, and inguinal creases. **Posterior landmarks** include the scapular spine, vertebral prominens, and gluteal cleft. Recognizing these external markers allows nurses to place stethoscope chest pieces over the correct heart valves or locate safe sites for intramuscular injections without guessing.

headings.title: Clinical Applications in Nursing Assessment and Documentation
headings.content: Accurate regional documentation protects patient safety and ensures clear communication among the multidisciplinary team. Vague descriptions like 'pain in the leg' fail to communicate severity or exact pathology, whereas specifying 'throbbing pain in the left calf' directs immediate clinical focus. When charting wounds, surgical incisions, or rashes, nurses must combine regional terminology with precise measurements to track healing progress accurately over time.
